listening.title: The first answer is a trap
listening.subtitle: The speaker says one answer, then changes it
rows: “Let's meet on Tuesday... **actually**, Wednesday is better.”
Writing Tuesday and moving to the next question
listening.caption: POV: you wrote “Tuesday”, but the speaker changed their mind 💀 One more signal: “on second thoughts”. When you hear it, stop your pen ✋ Has this trap ever caught you? Tell us in the comments 👇

listening.title: Is it 15 or 50?
listening.subtitle: -teen and -ty are the easiest pair to mix up
rows: fif**TEEN**: stress at the end, long sound
**FIF**ty: stress at the start, short sound
Listen to 13–19 and 30–90 in pairs for 5 minutes a day
listening.caption:
This mistake takes the most points in Section 1 😬

Mini test: say 14, 40, 17, 70 to a friend in any order. They write. Then switch 🔁

How many did you get right? Tell us in the comments 👇

listening.title: The word limit eats points
listening.subtitle: A right answer over the limit = 0
rows: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS → “a large garden”
**a / an / the** count as words too
listening.caption: Real talk: the limit is written at the start of every part, but half of people don't read it 👀 Make it a habit: circle the limit. And remember, a number like 25 is not a word, it is a number. Have you made this mistake? 👇

listening.title: A name spelled out loud
listening.subtitle: T-H-O-M-P-S-O-N. Which letter did you miss?
rows: Hearing the name and writing it from memory
Write only the **letters**, don't think about the word
listening.caption:
When you hear letters, your brain starts to “guess” the word. Don't let it 🧠

At the end, count the letters: if the speaker said 8 letters, you need 8 too ✅

Can you spell your name in English? 👇

listening.title: “Oh” = zero
listening.subtitle: In a phone number it is a number, not a letter
listening.caption: Phone numbers in Section 1 = free points 🎁 Life hack: write the number in groups of 3–4: 07 44 512. This way you don't get lost. Can you say your phone number in English? Try it 😄

listening.title: Read the questions first
listening.subtitle: If you read after the audio starts, it is too late
rows: Reading the questions after the audio starts
Read them in the **30 seconds** before each part
Guess the answer type: number, name, place
listening.caption:
Listening = 50% listening, 50% getting ready 🎯

Those 30 seconds are your most important time. Don't waste them checking old answers.

What do you do in that time? 👇

listening.title: Read the gap
listening.subtitle: Grammar tells you half of the answer
rows: after **at** → a time or a place
listening.caption:
If you know the answer type before the audio starts, your ear looks only for that 🔍

Challenge: in your next test, write N (number), P (place) or NM (name) next to each gap ✍️

Did your score change? Tell us in the comments 👇

listening.title: Don't forget the plural -s
listening.subtitle: Not “towel” but “towels”. The point is gone
listening.caption:
You often can't hear the -s, but grammar still needs it 👀

Rule: trust the sentence, not your ear. If there is a number or “some”, check the -s.

How many points has this mistake cost you? 😅

listening.title: Don't get lost on the map
listening.subtitle: Map labelling: find the entrance first
rows: Before the audio, find the **entrance** or **you are here**
Follow the speaker's path with your finger
listening.caption:
Map questions are the “boss level” of Section 2 🗺

Tip: don't think north is always at the top. Start walking from the place where the speaker starts.

Do you love or hate map questions? 👇

listening.title: Direction words
listening.subtitle: If you don't know them, the map question is lost
rows: **opposite** = on the other side, facing it
**at the far end** = at the very end
listening.caption: Bonus words: clockwise = the way a clock's hands move, halfway along = in the middle of the road 🧭 Save this and look at it again before your exam 🔖 Which word would you add? 👇

listening.title: A, B, C: you hear them all
listening.subtitle: In multiple choice only one is correct
rows: Choosing a word the moment you hear it
Look at the **meaning**, not the word
The right answer often comes as a **synonym**
listening.caption: Example: the option says “cheap”, but the audio says “it won't cost much” 💸 The wrong option is often said word for word. The right one is said in a different way. Remember this trap. Are multiple choice questions hard for you? 👇

listening.title: Know your synonyms
listening.subtitle: One word in the question, another in the audio
listening.caption:
Listening is really a synonym game 🎮

After each test, write 5 new pairs in your notebook. In 1 month you will have 100 📒

What is your favourite pair? 👇

listening.title: Don't get lost in Section 4
listening.subtitle: 10 questions, no break
rows: If you can't find it, **move on at once**
“**Moving on to...**” = a new question is near
listening.caption:
Losing 3 questions because of 1 is the most expensive mistake 💀

Practice: when you listen to a lecture and hear a signal word, tap the table once with your finger. It keeps you focused 👆

How does Section 4 go for you? 👇

listening.title: Signposts = your map
listening.subtitle: The speaker tells you what comes next
listening.caption:
When you hear these words, check where you are in the question list ✅

Then you never panic and think “which question am I on?”

Which other signal words do you know? 👇

listening.title: How to write dates
listening.subtitle: Write “March 3th” and the point is gone
listening.caption:
Months and days are where most spelling mistakes happen 📅

Quick test: write Wednesday, February and September now, then check. All correct? 😏

Write your result in the comments 👇

listening.title: Spelling mistake = 0 points
listening.subtitle: You heard it right but wrote it wrong
listening.caption:
These words appear at least once in every Cambridge book 📚

Once a week, do a small dictation: a friend says the words, you write. 5 minutes is enough.

Which word do you always get wrong? 👇

listening.title: What is “twelve fifty”?
listening.subtitle: The most common trap with money
rows: If £ or $ is in the question, **don't write it again**
listening.caption: Prices are a favourite topic in Section 1 💷 One more example: “a hundred and twenty” = 120, and “one twenty” can be 120 too. Look at the context. Have prices ever confused you? 👇

listening.title: Quarter to = 15 minutes before
listening.subtitle: “A quarter to nine” is not 9:15!
listening.caption: This mistake is very common, because many languages don't say time this way 🤯 How to remember: to = “before”, so there are 15 minutes left before 9. What time is it now? Write it in English 👇

listening.title: “Except” flips the meaning
listening.subtitle: Miss a negative word and your answer is the opposite
rows: **apart from, rather than, unless** work the same way
listening.caption:
These words are small, but they turn the answer 180° 🔄

Underline them on the question paper too. If the question has “NOT”, it is written in capital letters.

Which other “dangerous” words do you know? 👇

listening.title: Choose two letters
listening.subtitle: 2 rules for “Choose TWO letters” questions
rows: The order does not matter: **A, C** = **C, A**
If you know only one, **don't leave the other empty**
listening.caption:
An empty box = 0 for sure. A guess = a 20–25% chance 🎲

The maths is on your side 😄

Are these questions easy or hard for you? 👇

listening.title: Who said what?
listening.subtitle: Section 3: three people, three opinions
rows: In the first minute, match each **name + voice**
listening.caption: In Section 3 you listen for opinions, not single words 🎭 Practice: when two people argue in a podcast, write down who agrees with who. How is Section 3 for you? 👇

listening.title: “I suppose so, but...”
listening.subtitle: Is this a yes? Actually, no
listening.caption:
British people don't like to say a direct “no” 🫖

So knowing these soft phrases gives you points in Section 3.

Which other “soft no” do you know? 👇

listening.title: Flow chart = order
listening.subtitle: The process always follows the arrows
listening.caption:
In flow chart questions the answers come in order. They don't jump ✅

If you found answer 3, answer 4 comes after it. Don't look back.

Do flow charts feel easy to you? 👇

listening.title: The audio plays only once
listening.subtitle: If you wait to hear it again, it is gone
rows: Listening to the test 2–3 times when you practise
The second listening is only for **checking your mistakes**
listening.caption:
Practise like it is the real exam. Then the real exam feels like practice 💪

Today, listen to one Section once, then check with the transcript.

What was your result? 👇

listening.title: Only 2 minutes on the computer test
listening.subtitle: You don't get the 10 minutes of the paper test
rows: Type the answer in the box **at once**
listening.caption:
Computer-delivered IELTS is getting more popular 💻

Practise on a computer at home too. Do the official demo test at least once.

Which format did you choose? 👇

listening.title: Capital or small letters?
listening.subtitle: LONDON, london or London?
rows: Capital or small letters **don't change your score**
On the paper test, **ALL CAPITALS** is the safe way
Then **a** and **o** don't look the same
listening.caption:
A small detail, but if your handwriting is hard to read, you can lose points ✍️

On the computer test this is not a problem. The keyboard does the job.

How do you write? 👇

listening.title: The postcode trap
listening.subtitle: CB2 1TN: letters and numbers together
rows: Write only the **symbols**, don't think about the meaning
listening.caption:
Postcodes and addresses come up often in Section 1 🏠

Practice: find some UK postcodes online and read them to a friend as a dictation.

Which letters do you mix up? 👇

listening.title: Mixing up A, E, I
listening.subtitle: English letter names can trick your ear
listening.caption:
When a name is spelled out, these letters cause the most mistakes 😵‍💫

2 minutes a day: spell your name and your friends' names in English.

Spell your name in the comments 👇

listening.title: Completing a table
listening.subtitle: Row or column? Find out first
rows: Look at the empty column and expect **that type of information**
listening.caption:
In table questions the speaker often goes down the column, but you read across the row 🔀

If you know the direction first, half the job is done.

How are table questions for you? 👇

listening.title: Write what you hear
listening.subtitle: The synonym is in the question, not in the answer
rows: Answer = **the exact word** from the audio
listening.caption:
In Listening, don't be creative. Just copy 📝

It is the same in Reading: the answer is taken exactly from the text.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

listening.title: Site or sight?
listening.subtitle: They sound the same but mean different things
rows: Choose by the **meaning** of the sentence
listening.caption: Homophones are the hidden enemy of Listening 🥷 More examples: buy / by, right / write, hour / our. Write a homophone you know 👇

listening.title: “Wanna” = want to
listening.subtitle: Book English and audio English are not the same
rows: “**Wha-d'ya** wanna do?” = What do you want to do?
listening.caption:
In real life nobody speaks like a textbook 😄

Practice: listen to a podcast for 5 minutes a day, write what you hear and compare it with the transcript.

Which short form tricks you the most? 👇

listening.title: Small words disappear
listening.subtitle: You can hardly hear of, to, and
rows: Trying to hear every single word
Listen for the **stressed words**: nouns, verbs, numbers
listening.caption:
The answers are almost always in the stressed words 🎯

So don't panic if you did not hear “of”. Nouns and numbers are what matter.

What do you listen for? 👇

listening.title: Don't be afraid of accents
listening.subtitle: British, Australian, Canadian
listening.caption:
If you only watch American films, an Australian speaker will surprise you in the exam 🦘

Train your ear with different accents.

Which accent is the hardest for you? 👇

listening.title: 30 minutes of focus
listening.subtitle: By Section 4 your brain is tired
listening.caption:
Focus is like a muscle: it gets stronger when you train it 💪

A full test 2 times a week = you don't get tired in the exam.

How many minutes can you stay focused? 👇

listening.title: One mistake is not a reason to panic
listening.subtitle: Think about the last question and you lose 3 more
rows: Thinking about the question you missed
Write a guess and move on **at once**
Even with 1 mistake out of 40, **Band 8.5** is possible
listening.caption:
Listening is a marathon, not a sprint 🏃

Don't lose the whole section because of one question. Take a deep breath and go to the next one.

Have you ever panicked in the exam? 👇

listening.title: Don't leave it empty
listening.subtitle: You don't lose points for a wrong answer
rows: You did not hear it → the box is empty
Write a **word that makes sense** and fits the grammar
listening.caption:
In IELTS there is no “I don't know”. There is only a guess 😎

A word that fits the grammar and the context is often right.

Do you guess? 👇

listening.title: Less is safer
listening.subtitle: You wrote “the big park” and went over the limit
rows: If the answer is “park”, write only **park**
Add an adjective only if the **grammar** needs it
listening.caption:
An extra word = an extra risk ⚠️

Even if the word limit lets you write more, write only what is needed.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

listening.title: Is “3 bedrooms” OK?
listening.subtitle: The ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER question
listening.caption:
Writing a number as a word can push you over the limit 🔢

Digits are faster and safer.

Did you know this? ✅ or ❌ 👇

listening.title: Don't do the maths
listening.subtitle: Is “a third” 33% or 30%?
listening.caption: Listening is not a maths test 🧮 Useful pairs: a quarter = 25%, half = 50%, three quarters = 75%. Have you ever calculated and got it wrong? 👇

listening.title: Which year is it about?
listening.subtitle: Two similar numbers, only one is the answer
rows: The question is about this year → **450**
listening.caption: When you hear a number, don't write it at once. Check the time ⏳ Signal words: originally, now, last year, this year. Has this trap caught you? 👇

listening.title: Think of synonyms for each option
listening.subtitle: Option: “too expensive”. Audio: different words
rows: Think of **1–2 synonyms** for each option
listening.caption:
In matching questions the options are never said word for word 🔁

If you think of synonyms first, you will know them when the audio comes.

Add one more synonym 👇

listening.title: Don't mix up the places
listening.subtitle: Section 2: a guide talks about 5 places
rows: Make a mark each time you hear a **place name**
When the next name comes, **the last one is finished**
listening.caption:
Section 2 has a lot of information, but the order is clear 🗂

The place names are your “chapter titles”.

How do you do Section 2? 👇

listening.title: Write in short forms
listening.subtitle: If you write long words, you miss the next sentence
rows: Writing with full spelling while the audio plays
Write the full spelling **in the last minute**
listening.caption:
Let your ear keep working and your hand write faster ✍️⚡

You need this less on the computer test, but it helps a lot on the paper test.

What short forms do you use? 👇

listening.title: Both, neither, either
listening.subtitle: They change a multiple choice answer completely
rows: **both** = yes to the two of them
**neither** = no to the two of them
listening.caption:
“Neither of the options was suitable” = the two options were both no good 🙅

When you hear these words, think about the options again.

Do you mix these words up? 👇

listening.title: The main idea comes after “but”
listening.subtitle: Good side and bad side in a comparison
listening.caption:
Find out what the question asks: advantage or disadvantage? 🎯

One sentence has two answers, but only one fits the question.

Are these questions hard? 👇

listening.title: The old plan is a trap
listening.subtitle: After “We were going to...” comes a change
rows: **were going to, originally** = the old plan
“...in the hall, but it's being repaired, **so** the gym.”
listening.caption: Answer: gym, not hall 🏟 IELTS loves changing plans. Has this trap caught you? 👇

listening.title: A 4-step check
listening.subtitle: 2 minutes after the test = a few more points
rows: Is the number of words inside the **limit**?
listening.caption:
3 spelling mistakes = 3 points = a different band 😱

Save this list and use it after every test 🔖

Do you check your answers? 👇

listening.title: What comes after the gap?
listening.subtitle: Grammar tells you if you need an adjective or a noun
rows: Gap at the end → probably a **noun**
listening.caption:
Reading the grammar = finding half of the answer 🧩

This works in Listening and in Reading.

Does grammar help you? 👇

listening.title: Tests alone are not enough
listening.subtitle: If you remember the answers, new audio is still hard
rows: Doing the same test again and again
**15 minutes** of real English every day
listening.caption:
Your ear needs to get used to new voices 👂

Tests are for the exam format. Podcasts are for real listening.

Which podcast do you listen to? Share it 👇

listening.title: Dictation practice
listening.subtitle: You understand, but you can't write the words
rows: Stop after each sentence and write **every word**
listening.caption:
In 2 weeks your listening and your spelling get better together 📈

The simplest exercise, and the one people do the least.

Will you try it today? 👇

listening.title: Try shadowing
listening.subtitle: To understand fast speech, speak it yourself
listening.caption:
When your mouth learns the rhythm, your ear knows it too 🎶

Bonus: your Speaking pronunciation gets better as well.

Have you tried shadowing? 👇

listening.title: A mistake notebook
listening.subtitle: The same mistakes come back in every test
rows: In 3 weeks you will see your **main mistake type**
listening.caption:
Your score grows when you study your mistakes, not when you just do tests 🚀

Your own mistake notebook is the strongest study tool.

Do you have one? 👇

listening.title: Read the transcript
listening.subtitle: You got it wrong, but you don't know why
rows: Looking at the score and closing the book
Listen to the wrong questions again **with the transcript**
listening.caption:
This is where you grow the fastest 📈

Every test = 30 minutes of work + 15 minutes of checking.

Do you check your mistakes? 👇

listening.title: Section 1 matters too
listening.subtitle: If you think it is easy and relax, you lose points
rows: For Band 7+, Sections 1–2 must be almost **without mistakes**
Most points are lost on **spelling and numbers**
listening.caption:
Section 1 is free points. Don't give them away 🎁

Give even the easiest question your full attention.

How many mistakes do you usually make in Section 1? 👇

listening.title: Fast note taking
listening.subtitle: In Section 4 you can't write everything
listening.caption:
Catch only the word you need for the gap and shorten the rest ⚡

These symbols will help you at university too 🎓

What is your favourite symbol? 👇

listening.title: Listen to the end of the sentence
listening.subtitle: The correction often comes 1 second later
listening.caption:
People who hurry lose points ⏸

You heard the answer? Great. Now wait 1 second.

Has this happened to you? 👇

listening.title: Two answers = danger
listening.subtitle: “Card or cash”: only one word was needed
rows: Choose the one that **fits the question best**
listening.caption:
Two answers are usually marked as wrong ⚠️

Read the question again: what exactly does it ask?

Has this happened to you? 👇

listening.title: Not “Sat” but “Saturday”
listening.subtitle: Short forms are risky
rows: Only if you hear them in the audio: **BBC, UK, DVD**
listening.caption:
If you are not sure, write the full word ✍️

The full word takes 2 seconds. A mistake costs 1 point.

Which month do you always spell wrong? 👇

listening.title: Check your headphones
listening.subtitle: If the sound is low, the whole test is harder
rows: There is a **sound check** before the test
Set the volume **the way you like it**
If there is a problem, **raise your hand at once**
listening.caption:
On exam day, small things make a big difference 🎧

Don't be shy: if the sound is bad, you have the right to say so.

Have you had this problem in an exam? 👇

listening.title: Don't leave Listening for later
listening.subtitle: The ear improves slowly
listening.caption:
A daily habit is much stronger than a weekly marathon 🔥

Start today: 20 minutes, phone off.

How many minutes a day do you listen? 👇

listening.title: Trust your first feeling
listening.subtitle: “Too easy, it must be a trap” and you get it wrong
rows: Changing an answer you heard clearly
If the speaker doesn't correct it, **the first answer** is right
listening.caption:
Thinking too much also costs points 🧠💥

Sometimes IELTS asks a simple question and wants a simple answer.

Do you think too much? 👇

reading.title: Do you read everything?
reading.subtitle: 60 minutes, 3 texts, 40 questions. Not enough time
rows: Reading the text word by word from start to end
Skim for **2–3 minutes**: the title and the first sentences
Read the question and underline the **key word**
Read carefully only the paragraph you need
reading.caption: Real talk: Reading is not a speed test, it is a search test 🔍 Today's challenge: in your next test, use a timer and spend no more than 20 minutes on each text ⏱ If you do it, put ✅ in the comments 👇

reading.title: False or Not Given?
reading.subtitle: The question type where people lose the most points
rows: **TRUE**: the text agrees with the sentence
**NOT GIVEN**: the text says nothing about it
reading.caption: The golden rule: don't add what you know, trust only the text 📄 For FALSE, the text must have proof of the opposite. No proof = NOT GIVEN. Which one do you get wrong the most? 👇

reading.title: T/F/NG vs Y/N/NG
reading.subtitle: They look the same, but the question is different
rows: In Y/N/NG, look for **what the writer thinks**
reading.caption: In Yes/No questions, watch for phrases like I believe, arguably, it is clear that 👀 They show the writer's opinion. Did you know this? ✅ or ❌ 👇

reading.title: Don't look for the exact word
reading.subtitle: The question says “elderly”, the text says “senior citizens”
rows: Looking for the **exact** question word in the text
Think of **2–3 synonyms** for each key word
The exact same word is often **a trap**
reading.caption:
Reading is a synonym hunt 🎯

Practice: find 5 synonym pairs in today's test and write them in your notebook.

Write your most interesting pair in the comments 👇

reading.title: Which questions come in order?
reading.subtitle: If you know this, you find answers 2x faster
rows: **In order**: T/F/NG, Y/N/NG, multiple choice, sentence completion
reading.caption:
This rule saves a lot of time ⏱

For questions that come in order, you don't need to go back and search.

Did you know this? 👇

reading.title: The headings trap
reading.subtitle: You saw a key word and chose the heading. Wrong
rows: Choosing a heading because of one word
Heading = the **main idea** of the paragraph
reading.caption:
Matching headings is the “trickiest” IELTS question 🦊

Ask yourself: what is the whole paragraph about? Not one detail, but the big picture.

Are headings hard for you? 👇

reading.title: Headings: a smart order
reading.subtitle: You don't have to start with the first paragraph
rows: Do the **shortest** and clearest paragraphs first
**Cross out** the headings you have used
At the end, choose from the **2–3 that are left**
reading.caption:
The fewer options you have, the easier the question gets 📉

This method turns 15 minutes into 8.

Will you try it? 👇

reading.title: The word limit works in Reading too
reading.subtitle: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS: you wrote three
rows: Copy the answer **exactly** from the text
Changing the word form can also be **wrong**
reading.caption: If the text says pollution, don't write polluted ✍️ If the grammar needs a different form, you have found the wrong place. Have you made this mistake? 👇

reading.title: Summary with a word list
reading.subtitle: 10 words, 6 gaps
rows: What kind of word does the gap need: **noun, verb, adjective**?
Choose **by meaning** only from the right type
reading.caption:
Grammar cuts the options in half ✂️

After that, choosing is much easier.

Do you like summary questions? 👇

reading.title: A time plan
reading.subtitle: 30 minutes on the first text = 10 for the third
rows: When the time is up, **move to the next one**
reading.caption:
Passage 3 is the hardest, so keep the most time for it 🧗

Check the clock at the end of each part.

How do you plan your time? 👇

reading.title: Don't get stuck on one question
reading.subtitle: 5 minutes = 4 easy questions
rows: Sitting on a hard question for 5 minutes
If you can't find it in 1 minute, **mark it and move on**
reading.caption:
A hard question does not give more points 🤷

If you have time at the end, come back. If not, write a guess.

Which question type makes you stuck? 👇

reading.title: Skimming vs scanning
reading.subtitle: They are two different things
rows: **Skimming**: reading fast for the main idea
In scanning your eyes **don't read**, they only search
reading.caption:
If you can do them fast, you will have enough time in Reading ⚡

Scanning practice: find all the numbers in a news article in 30 seconds.

Did you do it? 👇

reading.title: Find numbers and names
reading.subtitle: They are easy to see in the text
rows: Names that start with a **capital letter**
reading.caption:
If the question has “1987” or “Dr Wilson”, don't read the text from the start 🙅

Move your eyes over the text and look only for that.

Do you scan? 👇

reading.title: The multiple choice trap
reading.subtitle: The option has the exact words from the text. Be careful
rows: An option that repeats the text word for word is often **a trap**
The right answer gives the meaning in **different words**
reading.caption:
IELTS loves to trick you with words you know 🎣

A word you know is not always the right answer.

Has this trap caught you? 👇

reading.title: Some ≠ all
reading.subtitle: Words about amount change the answer
reading.caption:
A small word, a big difference 🔬

Always compare the amount in the question and in the text.

Which other “dangerous” words do you know? 👇

reading.title: Don't be afraid of Not Given
reading.subtitle: No proof does not mean FALSE
rows: Choosing FALSE because “it must be so”
The text does not say yes or no = **NOT GIVEN**
reading.caption:
NOT GIVEN does not mean “I could not find it”. It means “it is not in the text” 🕵️

Check the text well, then choose it with confidence.

Is NOT GIVEN hard for you? 👇

reading.title: Forget what you know
reading.subtitle: True in life ≠ true in the text
rows: The text says nothing about it → **NOT GIVEN**
reading.caption:
In Reading the only judge is the text ⚖️

Leave what you know at the door 🚪

Have you made this mistake? 👇

reading.title: Matching information
reading.subtitle: “Which paragraph contains...?”
rows: Reading the text again for each question
By then you **already** know the text well
reading.caption:
These questions don't come in order and take the most time ⏳

Do the other questions first and get to know the text.

What order do you use? 👇

reading.title: The scientist and their opinion
reading.subtitle: 5 names, 7 opinions
rows: Read the **2–3 sentences** around the name
One name can appear **more than once**
reading.caption:
In matching features questions, getting ready is half the win 🏆

Marking the names takes 1 minute but saves 5.

Will you try it? 👇

reading.title: Sentence endings
reading.subtitle: The meaning is right, but the grammar doesn't fit
rows: First remove the endings that **don't fit the grammar**
Compare the rest with the **meaning of the text**
A sentence can sound logical but **not be in the text**
reading.caption:
A two-step check = fewer mistakes ✅

Grammar is the fastest filter.

How are these questions for you? 👇

reading.title: Diagram labelling
reading.subtitle: A machine in the picture, a long description in the text
rows: Find the **words given** on the diagram in the text
reading.caption:
From top to bottom, or from left to right 🧭

Diagram questions are often some of the easiest points.

Do you like diagram questions? 👇

reading.title: A new word is not a stop sign
reading.subtitle: Don't let one word stop the whole text
rows: If the question is not about that word, **move on**
reading.caption:
Even in our own language we don't know every word, but we still understand 😉

The sentences before and after often explain the meaning.

Do you use the dictionary a lot? 👇

reading.title: The text explains itself
reading.subtitle: An explanation hides next to the hard word
rows: An explanation between commas or in **brackets**
reading.caption:
The text wants to help you. Just notice these signals 🤝

Academic texts have a lot of these explanations.

Have you noticed this? 👇

reading.title: Although = be careful
reading.subtitle: Linking words show the logic of the sentence
reading.caption: Linking words are the road signs of the text 🚦 therefore, as a result = a result. Watch for them too. Which other linking words do you know? 👇

reading.title: Don't change the form
reading.subtitle: The text says “pollution”, you write “polluted”
rows: Changing the form of the word
Copy the answer **in the form used in the text**
If the form doesn't fit, **look in another place**
reading.caption:
In completion questions the answer is always ready in the text 📦

You need to find it, not make it.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

reading.title: Passage 3 has easy points too
reading.subtitle: Use a plan, not fear
rows: Start with the first **summary or multiple choice** questions
Losing **easy points** because of one hard question
reading.caption:
Don't panic when you see Passage 3 😌

It is longer, but half of the questions are of medium difficulty.

How is Passage 3 for you? 👇

reading.title: Questions first, then the text
reading.subtitle: If not, you read the text twice
rows: Read the questions fast and underline the **key words**
Find the **right place** for each question
reading.caption:
This way you read the text once and have enough time ⏰

It is the simplest method, and it works best.

What order do you use? 👇

reading.title: The main purpose question
reading.subtitle: “What is the writer's main purpose?”
rows: Choosing one detail as the answer
reading.caption:
This question is about the whole text, not one paragraph 🌍

Look at the big picture.

Are these questions easy or hard for you? 👇

reading.title: “So-called” is not respect
reading.subtitle: Words show the writer's tone
reading.caption:
These words are the key in Yes/No/Not Given questions 🔑

What does the writer believe? What does the writer doubt? These words tell you.

Save this 🔖

reading.title: No extra time to copy in Reading
reading.subtitle: The paper test gives no extra 10 minutes
rows: Leaving your answers on the question paper
Write the answers on the answer sheet **at once**
On the **computer test** this is not a problem
reading.caption:
Not like Listening: in Reading you get 0 minutes to copy answers ⏰

Many people find this out in the exam 😱

Did you know? 👇

reading.title: Use copy and paste
reading.subtitle: How to stop spelling mistakes on the computer test
rows: Typing the answer letter by letter
reading.caption:
This is one of the biggest advantages of computer IELTS 💻

Try it at home in the official demo test.

Which format did you choose? 👇

reading.title: Helpers on the computer test
reading.subtitle: Most people don't use them
rows: **Notes**: add a note to a paragraph
reading.caption:
Don't see these tools for the first time on exam day 🙈

Practise with the official demo test first.

Which tool do you use? 👇

reading.title: Read faster
reading.subtitle: You understand, but you are too slow
rows: Don't say **every word** in your head
reading.caption:
Learn to read groups of words with your eyes 👀

In 1 month you will be much faster.

How many minutes do you need for one article? 👇

reading.title: Only tests = no progress
reading.subtitle: You do a test every day, but your score doesn't grow
rows: Find the **proof** in the text for every mistake
The reason: **a synonym, time, or not understanding**?
reading.caption:
Your score grows when you study your mistakes, not when you do more tests 📈

1 test + 20 minutes of checking > 3 tests with no checking.

Do you check your mistakes? 👇

reading.title: Academic Word List
reading.subtitle: significant, subsequent, comprise...
rows: A **big part** of Reading texts is made of these words
reading.caption:
You can learn the whole list in 2 months 🗓

These words give you points in Writing too.

Have you heard of the AWL? 👇

reading.title: Read around the number
reading.subtitle: The text has several dates
rows: Writing the first number you see
Read the **whole sentence** around the number
Is it the start date, the end date or a **date of change**?
reading.caption:
Similar numbers are a natural trap 🪤

Underline what the question really asks.

Has this trap caught you? 👇

reading.title: The topic sentence secret
reading.subtitle: The main idea of a paragraph is usually at the start
rows: Read the **first sentence** of the paragraph
If you need to, read the **second sentence** too
If you are not sure, look at the **last sentence**
reading.caption:
Academic texts are written with this rule 📐

It saves a lot of time in headings questions.

Did you know this? 👇

reading.title: Spot the paraphrase
reading.subtitle: The question and the text say one thing in different words
reading.caption:
The Reading test is really a paraphrase test 🔁

Write down 5 pairs after each test.

Which pair did you find today? 👇

reading.title: Top synonyms
reading.subtitle: They come up again and again in Reading
reading.caption:
If you know these pairs, many questions open up 🔓

Save this and repeat it before your exam 🔖

Add one more pair 👇

reading.title: Don't leave it empty
reading.subtitle: Time is up and 5 questions are empty
rows: In the last minute, write **a guess** for all of them
reading.caption:
You don't lose points for wrong answers, so a guess is a free chance 😎

The maths is on your side.

Do you guess? 👇

reading.title: Skip the brackets
reading.subtitle: (see Figure 2), (Smith, 2019)
rows: Sometimes the **name or date** you need is there
reading.caption:
Brackets usually show a source, but sometimes they hold the answer 🎁

Decide by the question type.

Have you noticed this? 👇

reading.title: A long sentence: 4 lines
reading.subtitle: At the end you forget the start
rows: The part between commas is **extra** information
reading.caption:
First the main idea: who did what? Then the details 🧩

Academic sentences are long, but their structure is simple.

Are long sentences hard for you? 👇

reading.title: Where is the summary?
reading.subtitle: Which part of the text does the summary cover?
rows: Read the summary's **title and first sentence**
Find the **similar part** in the text
reading.caption:
The summary often follows the order of the text ➡️

When you find the first answer, the others are close.

Do you like summary questions? 👇

reading.title: Don't think too much
reading.subtitle: The answer looks clear, but you chose a different one
rows: “Too easy, it must be a trap”
If the text gives **clear proof**, trust it
reading.caption:
Looking for traps everywhere also costs points 🧠💥

There is proof = there is an answer.

Do you think too much? 👇

reading.title: A good key word
reading.subtitle: You can't search with “the” or “important”
reading.caption:
Rare words don't turn into synonyms in the text, so you find them fast 🎯

Choosing key words is the first Reading skill.

How do you choose them? 👇

reading.title: Each question has its own method
reading.subtitle: Don't read the same way for every question
reading.caption:
Know the question type and choose the right method 🛠

This is the secret of going from Band 6 to Band 7.

Which question type is the hardest for you? 👇

reading.title: When two options look right
reading.subtitle: You can't decide in multiple choice
rows: Compare each option with the text **word by word**
One of them is only **partly** right
reading.caption:
Partly right = wrong ❌

The right answer answers the whole question.

Does this happen to you a lot? 👇

reading.title: 60 minutes of focus
reading.subtitle: In Passage 3 you read one sentence 3 times
rows: Do the full test **with no break**
reading.caption:
Your brain is like an athlete: it needs training 🏋️

Breakfast matters too: it is hard to focus when you are hungry 🍳

How many minutes can you read with full focus? 👇

reading.title: Don't skip the first paragraph
reading.subtitle: 30 seconds = a map of the whole text
rows: Not reading the introduction to save time
The introduction tells you **what the text is about**
It also shows the **structure** of the text
reading.caption:
Spend 30 seconds and all the next questions get easier 🗺

It is the cheapest investment.

Do you read the introduction? 👇

reading.title: Find the structure of the text
reading.subtitle: If you know it, you know where the answer is
reading.caption:
When you skim, find out which structure the text has 🧭

Then you know where to go when a question comes.

Have you tried this? 👇

reading.title: Initially = at the start
reading.subtitle: Time signals in history texts
rows: **initially, originally, at first** = at the start
reading.caption:
Find the part that fits the time in the question 📅

In history texts these signals are the address of the answer.

Save this 🔖

reading.title: Cause and result
reading.subtitle: Was A the cause, or B?
rows: **A led to B** = A is the cause
**A resulted from B** = B is the cause
If the direction is the opposite = **FALSE**
reading.caption:
Look at which way the arrow points 🏹

This is a favourite T/F/NG trap.

Has this trap caught you? 👇

reading.title: Not as ... as
reading.subtitle: Compare how much
reading.caption: Text: A is not as effective as B. Question: A is more effective → FALSE ❌ Always underline the words that show how much. Which other comparing phrases do you know? 👇

reading.title: May ≠ will
reading.subtitle: The difference between maybe and for sure
rows: The text says maybe, the question says for sure → **not TRUE**
reading.caption:
This is the favourite trap of Yes/No/Not Given 🪤

Look at how sure the writer is.

Did you know this? 👇

reading.title: “Novel” is not only a book
reading.subtitle: Words with more than one meaning
reading.caption: Choose the meaning from the context 🔍 Bonus: an issue can also be one copy of a magazine. Which other “tricky” words do you know? 👇

reading.title: Read for fun
reading.subtitle: Only exam texts = slow progress
rows: Read about what you like: **football, technology, history**
Your speed and vocabulary **grow on their own**
reading.caption:
Your brain doesn't get tired when you read something interesting 🧠✨

Today, read one English article about your favourite topic.

Which topic will you choose? 👇

reading.title: Your own synonym list
reading.subtitle: One synonym pair from each mistake
rows: Find the **proof sentence** in the text for the wrong answer
Write the **synonym pair** in your notebook
reading.caption:
This list is more useful than any list on the internet 📒

Because it is made from your own mistakes.

Will you start today? 👇

reading.title: Slight ≠ significant
reading.subtitle: There is a change, but the size is different
reading.caption:
Words that show size come up a lot in T/F/NG 📏

Compare the size in the question and in the text.

Save this 🔖

reading.title: Check every part
reading.subtitle: A sentence that is half right is not TRUE
reading.caption:
Check each piece of information in the question one by one ✅✅

If one part is wrong, the whole sentence is wrong.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

reading.title: The answer is in two sentences
reading.subtitle: this, it, such point back to the sentence before
rows: Read the sentences **before and after** too
Find out what **this, it, such** mean here
reading.caption:
Sometimes the answer is not in one sentence. It is spread over two 🧩

Put the full meaning together.

Have you seen this? 👇

reading.title: No new methods in the exam
reading.subtitle: Don't test today a strategy you saw yesterday
rows: Learning a **new method** 1 day before the exam
Use only the method you have **practised**
Try a new method in **5 tests** first
reading.caption:
The exam is not a place for experiments 🧪

A method you trust = a calm mind.

What do you do before an exam? 👇

reading.title: General is not easy
reading.subtitle: The texts are simpler, but you need more right answers
rows: In General there is **less room for mistakes**
reading.caption:
Thinking General Training is easy and not preparing is a big mistake 😬

Take both formats seriously.

Which format will you take? 👇

writing.title: No overview? Band 5
writing.subtitle: The most important sentence in Task 1
rows: Writing every number from the graph one by one
“**Overall**, car use rose steadily, while bus travel declined.”
writing.caption: With no overview, your Task Achievement stays at 5.0 or lower 😬 Make it a habit: look at the graph for 1 minute and ask yourself: what is the biggest change? Do you write an overview? 👇

writing.title: No opinions in Task 1
writing.subtitle: Just write what you see
writing.caption:
If the graph gives no reason, you should not give one 🙅

In Task 1, work like a camera, not like a journalist 📸

Have you made this mistake? 👇

writing.title: Don't copy the question
writing.subtitle: Copied words are not counted
rows: The graph **shows the number of** tourists...
The line chart **illustrates how many** people visited...
writing.caption: Paraphrase = showing good vocabulary from the very first sentence ✨ Ready pairs: number of → how many, percentage → proportion. How do you start? 👇

writing.title: Increased, increased...
writing.subtitle: The same verb again = a low vocabulary score
writing.caption: Use a different verb in each sentence, but make sure the meaning fits 🎯 plummeted = fell very fast. Don't use it for a small fall. Save this 🔖

writing.title: How much? How fast?
writing.subtitle: “Sales increased.” Not enough
writing.caption:
Verb + adverb + number = a perfect Task 1 sentence 💯

Practice: today, describe one graph in 3 sentences with this formula.

Write it in the comments and I will check it 👇

writing.title: You don't need every number
writing.subtitle: 24 numbers = a list, not a text
rows: Writing every number from the table
**The biggest, the smallest**, the start, the end
writing.caption:
The examiner wants to see that you can choose 🧠

Picking the important information = Band 7.

How many numbers do you usually write? 👇

writing.title: Compare!
writing.subtitle: Each category alone = a weak Task 1
writing.caption:
Comparing is the heart of Task 1 ❤️

Put at least 2 comparisons in each body paragraph.

What is your favourite comparing phrase? 👇

writing.title: No time in a pie chart
writing.subtitle: Not “increased”, but shares
writing.caption:
If there is only one pie chart, don't use verbs of change ⚠️

If there are two pie charts (2000 and 2020), then you can.

Are pie charts easy or hard for you? 👇

writing.title: Process = passive
writing.subtitle: The active voice does not fit a process
writing.caption:
Overview: how many steps, where it starts and where it ends 🔄

A process diagram is the easiest Task 1 to prepare for.

Do you like process tasks? 👇

writing.title: Language for map tasks
writing.subtitle: Before and after: what changed?
rows: **was replaced by** = a new thing was built in its place
writing.caption:
Overview: how much did the area change? Did it become more like a city? 🏙

Map tasks are rare, but they are hard if you are not ready.

Save this 🔖

writing.title: 20 minutes for Task 1
writing.subtitle: Task 2 gives twice as many points
writing.caption:
20 minutes are over? Finish Task 1, even if it is not perfect ⏰

Every point in Task 2 is worth more.

Which task do you start with? 👇

writing.title: Under 250 = a penalty
writing.subtitle: 230 words lowers your Task Response
writing.caption:
You don't need to write too much: 400 words = more mistakes 😅

Find out how many words you write in one line by hand.

How many words do you usually write? 👇

writing.title: Every part of the question
writing.subtitle: “Discuss both views AND give your opinion”
rows: Your opinion = **in the introduction and conclusion**
writing.caption:
If you miss one part, you can't get more than Band 6 🚧

Reading the question twice takes 30 seconds, but it saves your band.

Do you underline the question? 👇

writing.title: 4 types of Task 2 question
writing.subtitle: Each one needs its own structure
writing.caption:
Find the question type in 10 seconds, then make a plan 🗺

The same template for every question = Task Response 6.

Which type is the hardest for you? 👇

writing.title: Where is your position?
writing.subtitle: You gave two sides, but not your opinion
rows: Staying in the middle and hiding your opinion
writing.caption:
The examiner looks for your opinion 🔎

If your opinion changes in the middle, your Coherence score goes down too.

Do you choose a clear position? 👇

writing.title: Introduction = 2 sentences
writing.subtitle: An 80-word introduction = wasted time
rows: **Your opinion** or the plan of the essay
writing.caption:
You don't need a long introduction with history and “Nowadays” 🙅

Most points are in the body paragraphs.

How many sentences is your introduction? 👇

writing.title: The PEEL formula
writing.subtitle: Don't start a body paragraph with an example
writing.caption:
Every body paragraph in this order = Coherence 7+ 🧱

Today's practice: write one paragraph with PEEL.

Post it in the comments and I will look at it 👇

writing.title: An idea with no example is weak
writing.subtitle: No proof = Task Response 6
rows: “In **Finland**, where homework is minimal, students rank among the best.”
writing.caption:
Not general sentences, but a real situation 🎯

An example can be a country, a study or your own experience.

What is your favourite example? 👇

writing.title: No fake statistics
writing.subtitle: “87% of students...” Says who?
writing.caption:
The examiner sees fake statistics at once 🕵️

A personal or general example is safer and easier to believe.

Have you ever made up a statistic? 😅

writing.title: No new ideas in the conclusion
writing.subtitle: A new argument = lower Coherence
rows: A new idea that appears first in the conclusion
writing.caption: Start with In conclusion or To sum up and finish in 2 sentences 🏁 The conclusion is a short summary of your ideas, not a new chapter. How many sentences is your conclusion? 👇

writing.title: Moreover, Furthermore...
writing.subtitle: A linking word in every sentence = a robot
rows: Sometimes **This, Such, As a result** is enough
writing.caption:
Coherence = a natural flow, not a list of linking words 🌊

Practice: take out half of the linking words from your essay and read it again.

Is it better? 👇

writing.title: “People” 15 times
writing.subtitle: Repeating words kills your vocabulary score
writing.caption:
But don't use a synonym if the meaning does not really fit ⚠️

A correct synonym > a beautiful synonym.

Which word do you repeat the most? 👇

writing.title: Don't → do not
writing.subtitle: No short forms in academic writing
rows: Short forms are OK only in **a letter to a friend**
writing.caption:
A small detail, but the examiner sees it 👀

When you finish, look for apostrophes (') and check them.

Do you make this mistake? 👇

writing.title: “You should” is not academic
writing.subtitle: What to use in place of you and we
rows: Use **I** only for your opinion: I believe...
writing.caption:
Academic style = not personal, but clear 🎓

This makes your Task 2 sound more formal at once.

Do you use “you”? 👇

writing.title: Only simple sentences = 6.0
writing.subtitle: You need different grammar structures
writing.caption:
A complex sentence with a mistake = a low score. A simple sentence with no mistakes = a medium score 🤔

Use a mix of the two.

What is your favourite complex structure? 👇

writing.title: The formula for “if” sentences
writing.subtitle: Don't mix the tenses
rows: If taxes rise, people **will** drive less.
If cities **had** more parks, residents **would** be healthier.
writing.caption:
“If” sentences are perfect for giving solutions in Task 2 💡

Use at least 1 in every essay.

Write an example and I will check it 👇

writing.title: The education? No
writing.subtitle: Many languages have no articles, so this mistake is common
writing.caption:
A general idea = no article. A specific thing = the 🎯

This rule can raise your Grammar score by 0.5.

Are articles hard for you? 👇

writing.title: Informations? No!
writing.subtitle: These words have no plural
writing.caption: informations, advices, researches are some of the most common mistakes 😬 Save this and look for these words when you check your essay 🔖 Which one did you get wrong before? 👇

writing.title: “The number of” has
writing.subtitle: Subject-verb agreement
writing.caption:
“The number of” is used a lot in Task 1, so this mistake is expensive 💸

The number = one number, so the verb is singular.

Did you know this? 👇

writing.title: Don't join with a comma
writing.subtitle: The comma splice is a classic mistake
rows: Technology is useful**,** it saves time.
writing.caption:
You can't join two full sentences with only a comma 🚫

Use a linking word, a semicolon or a full stop.

Do you make this mistake? 👇

writing.title: Clichés lower your score
writing.subtitle: “Every coin has two sides”
writing.caption:
The examiner has seen these phrases hundreds of times 🥱

A clear and logical sentence is worth more than a pretty cliché.

Which cliché have you used? 😅

writing.title: A hard word ≠ a high score
writing.subtitle: Ubiquitous, plethora, quintessential...
rows: A hard word when you are not sure of the meaning
The right **collocation** + a simple word = Band 7
writing.caption:
A hard word used in the wrong way lowers your score 📉

Before you use a new word in an essay, see it in 3 example sentences.

Have you tried using hard words? 👇

writing.title: Make a research? No
writing.subtitle: The words are right, but they don't go together
writing.caption: Collocations are the key to Band 7 and 8 🔑 Bonus: meet demand, make a mistake, take measures. Save this 🔖

writing.title: A 5-minute plan
writing.subtitle: With no plan, you run out of ideas in the middle
writing.caption:
These 5 minutes save 35 minutes ⏳

People who plan don't cross out and start again.

Do you make a plan? 👇

writing.title: The last 3 minutes
writing.subtitle: A fast check before you finish
writing.caption:
These 3 minutes can raise your Grammar score by 0.5 📈

Look only for the mistakes you often make.

Do you leave time for checking? 👇

writing.title: Use paragraphs
writing.subtitle: One long paragraph = Coherence 5.0
writing.caption:
Leave an empty line between paragraphs 👀

The examiner sees the structure the moment they look at your essay.

How many paragraphs does your essay have? 👇

writing.title: 1 paragraph = 1 idea
writing.subtitle: 4 thin ideas < 2 deep ideas
writing.caption:
Depth matters more than the number of ideas 🌊

For Task Response 7+ your ideas must be fully developed.

How many ideas do you write? 👇

writing.title: Advantages outweigh?
writing.subtitle: This question asks for an opinion, not a list
writing.caption:
When you see the word “outweigh”, you need a clear answer ⚖️

Just listing advantages and disadvantages = Band 6.

How is this question type for you? 👇

writing.title: Make the solution clear
writing.subtitle: “The government should do something.” What?
rows: “Councils could introduce **free bus passes** for students.”
writing.caption:
A clear solution = a high Task Response 🛠

A general solution does not convince the examiner.

What is your best solution example? 👇

writing.title: Two questions = equal answers
writing.subtitle: “Why? Is it positive or negative?”
rows: One sentence for the second question
A short answer to **the two questions** in the introduction
writing.caption:
If one part is weak, your Task Response goes down 📉

Balance is the key.

Are two-part questions hard for you? 👇

writing.title: Stay on topic
writing.subtitle: The question is about online learning, you write about technology
rows: After each paragraph ask: **does this answer the question?**
Use the **key words** in every paragraph
writing.caption:
Underline the exact topic of the question and stay with it 🎯

Writing about a wide topic is easy, but it gives no points.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

writing.title: All young people? No
writing.subtitle: Saying “all” makes your idea weak
rows: “**All** young people are addicted to phones.”
“**Many** young people **tend to** spend too much time on phones.”
writing.caption:
Careful language = a sign of Band 7+ 🎓

Academic writing has very few 100% statements.

Do you use “all” a lot? 👇

writing.title: You need the passive too
writing.subtitle: All active sentences = all the same
writing.caption:
When it is not important who does the action, use the passive 🔄

It shows that you can use different grammar.

Do you use the passive? 👇

writing.title: Why? And then what?
writing.subtitle: You gave an idea but did not explain it
rows: “...because it shows unrealistic images, which **can lower** self-esteem.”
writing.caption:
Answer these two questions after every idea = a deep paragraph 🧠

This is the fastest way to raise your Task Response.

Will you try it? 👇

writing.title: Get the letter tone right
writing.subtitle: General Training: 3 tones
writing.caption:
“Dear Sir” to a friend is funny. “Hi!” to a manager is dangerous 😅

First find out who you are writing to.

Which tone is hard for you? 👇

writing.title: 3 bullets = 3 paragraphs
writing.subtitle: Miss one and you get Band 5
writing.caption:
This is the most common mistake in the General Training letter 📮

When you finish, check all 3 bullets ✅✅✅

Are you taking General? 👇

writing.title: The reason for the letter in the first sentence
writing.subtitle: After 3 paragraphs it is still not clear
rows: “I'm writing to tell you some **exciting news**!”
writing.caption:
The first sentence tells the reader what the letter is about 📬

This matters for Task Achievement.

How do you start? 👇

writing.title: A complaint: polite but firm
writing.subtitle: “You are lazy!” does not belong in a formal letter
writing.caption:
Be firm and polite together 🤝

A rude tone = low Task Achievement.

Save this 🔖

writing.title: “From 1990 year”? No
writing.subtitle: Write numbers the right way
writing.caption:
Task 1 has a lot of numbers, so there can be a lot of mistakes 🔢

Learn these 4 forms by heart.

Which one did you get wrong before? 👇

writing.title: Tenses in Task 1
writing.subtitle: A 2010–2020 graph is not in the present tense
writing.caption:
Choose the tense by the years on the graph 📅

A tense mistake hurts the whole text.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

writing.title: Language for the future
writing.subtitle: You wrote “will increase” 5 times
writing.caption:
Different phrases = better Lexical Resource ⬆️

Graphs about the future (2030, 2050) come up often.

Save this 🔖

writing.title: Just under half
writing.subtitle: How do you write 49.7%?
writing.caption:
“About” language makes your text more natural 🌿

Use a mix of exact numbers and “about” phrases.

Do you use these phrases? 👇

writing.title: Spelling mistakes
writing.subtitle: Small, but many of them cost points
writing.caption:
Write each of these words 5 times ✏️

You need them in almost every Task 2.

Which one do you always get wrong? 👇

writing.title: Can people read your handwriting?
writing.subtitle: A word nobody can read = a mistake
rows: Write clearly and cross out mistakes with **one line**
writing.caption:
The examiner does not guess: if they can't read it, it does not count 🙈

The computer test has no such problem, and it shows your word count.

Which format did you choose? 👇

writing.title: Reading samples is not enough
writing.subtitle: You read 50 Band 9 essays but wrote none
rows: **2 essays** a week, with a timer
writing.caption:
Writing gets better only by writing ✍️

Today, take 40 minutes and write one Task 2.

If you write it, put ✅ in the comments 👇

writing.title: The same mistakes
writing.subtitle: You write every day, but the mistakes come back
rows: Write down your **3 main mistakes** from each essay
In the next essay, watch **only for those**
writing.caption:
With no feedback, mistakes become habits 🔁

A teacher, a friend or you: someone must check.

What is your most common mistake? 👇

writing.title: No ideas?
writing.subtitle: You read the question and your mind is empty
writing.caption:
Think about the topic from these sides and find one effect for each 🧠

You get 4–5 ideas in 1 minute.

Try it: write 3 ideas about “Online shopping” 👇

writing.title: Top Task 2 topics
writing.subtitle: They come back again and again, so be ready
writing.caption:
Get 15 key words and 3 examples ready for each topic 📒

Even if you get a new topic in the exam, these words will help.

Which topic is the hardest for you? 👇

writing.title: Don't ask, answer
writing.subtitle: Questions to the reader are not academic
rows: “But is this really true? Who knows?”
“The impact of technology on children **remains a subject of debate**.”
writing.caption:
An essay is a place for answers, not questions ❓➡️❗

Write the same idea as a statement.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

writing.title: No exclamation marks!!!
writing.subtitle: Show feeling with words
rows: Exclamation marks only in **a letter to a friend**
writing.caption:
An academic text is calm but strong 💪

Show a strong idea with strong words, not with marks.

Do you use exclamation marks? 😅

writing.title: An essay with no conclusion
writing.subtitle: Time is up and there is no conclusion
rows: No conclusion = lower **Task Response and Coherence**
If you are short of time, **make the body shorter**
Even 1 sentence helps: “**In conclusion**, I firmly believe...”
writing.caption:
Never hand in an essay with no conclusion 🏁

In the last 5 minutes, check that your conclusion is there.

Has this happened to you? 👇

writing.title: The 4 marking criteria
writing.subtitle: Know how you are marked
writing.caption:
Each one is 25%. If you forget one, your whole score goes down ⚖️

Mark your own essay from these 4 sides.

Which one is your strongest? 👇

speaking.title: Don't stop at “Yes.”
speaking.subtitle: A one-word answer in Part 1 kills your Fluency
rows: **Example:** “Last week I made plov for my family.”
speaking.caption: The formula is simple: answer + reason + example = 15–20 seconds 🎯 Practice: answer “Do you like music?” with this formula in the comments, or leave a voice message 🎙 I will show the best answer in the next post 👀

speaking.title: Part 1: 1 minute is too long
speaking.subtitle: The examiner stopped you. Why?
rows: Talking for **1 minute** about a simple question
In Part 1 an answer is **15–20 seconds**
speaking.caption:
In Part 1 the examiner must ask many questions, and time is short ⏱

2–3 sentences = the perfect length.

Do you say too much or too little in Part 1? 👇

speaking.title: A memorised answer = 0
speaking.subtitle: The examiner hears it at once
rows: Your voice is **flat** and your speed is not natural
Prepare ideas, but make the sentences **new every time**
speaking.caption:
A natural mistake is better than a memorised perfect answer 💯

If the examiner hears a memorised answer, they change the topic.

Have you ever memorised an answer? 😅

speaking.title: Don't say “I don't know”
speaking.subtitle: Speaking tests your language, not your knowledge
rows: “That's an interesting question, I've **never really thought about it**, but...”
speaking.caption:
Think of something to say, even if you make it up 😉

The examiner tests your English, not your ideas.

Save this 🔖

speaking.title: 5 seconds of silence = minus
speaking.subtitle: Fill the pause in a natural way
speaking.caption:
But don't say “umm, ahh” too often ⚠️

These phrases give your brain 2 seconds, and they sound natural.

Which one do you use? 👇

speaking.title: Part 2: plan in 1 minute
speaking.subtitle: You get the card and don't know what to write?
rows: **2–3 key words** for each point on the card
Add **a feeling** and one interesting detail
speaking.caption:
This is enough for a 2-minute talk 🎤

Practice: take any Part 2 card, plan for 1 minute, speak for 2 minutes.

How did it go? 👇

speaking.title: Nothing to say after 1 minute
speaking.subtitle: How to speak for 2 minutes in Part 2
rows: A feeling: “**What I remember most is**...”
speaking.caption:
5 W questions + a feeling = 2 easy minutes ⏱

Make each point longer with these questions.

Can you speak for 2 minutes? 👇

speaking.title: A story, not a list
speaking.subtitle: “It was in 2019. It was nice.”
rows: **The surprise**: something you did not expect
speaking.caption:
A story is interesting to listen to, and it helps your Fluency 📖

The examiner is a person too and likes a good story 😄

What is your best story about? 👇

speaking.title: Tenses in Part 2
speaking.subtitle: A past event is not in the present tense
rows: Watch the **verb tense** on the card
speaking.caption:
The card tells you which tense to use 🃏

A tense mistake lowers your Grammar score.

Have you made this mistake? 👇

speaking.title: Part 3 ≠ Part 1
speaking.subtitle: “Because it's easy.” is not enough
speaking.caption:
In Part 3, speak for 30–45 seconds 🎙

Here the examiner looks at how deeply you can think.

Is Part 3 hard for you? 👇

speaking.title: Part 3 = society
speaking.subtitle: The question is general, but you talk only about you
speaking.caption:
Part 3 questions are about society, generations and governments 🌍

A personal example is OK, but after a general idea.

Did you know this difference? 👇

speaking.title: You can ask again
speaking.subtitle: If you don't understand, don't guess
speaking.caption:
Answering the wrong question is much worse than asking again 🙅

In Part 3 the examiner can also explain the question in a different way.

Are you shy to ask again? 👇

speaking.title: Your accent is not a problem
speaking.subtitle: What matters is being easy to understand
rows: You **don't need** a British or American accent
You are marked on **stress, intonation and clear sounds**
You can get **Band 8** with your own accent
speaking.caption:
Speaking less because you are afraid of your accent is the biggest mistake 🤐

Speak more, speak more clearly.

Does your accent worry you? 👇

speaking.title: W and V
speaking.subtitle: “Wery vell” is a classic mistake
rows: **W**: round lips, the teeth don't touch
**V**: the top teeth touch the bottom lip
Practice: “**We visited a very wet village**.”
speaking.caption:
Practise for 2 minutes a day in front of a mirror 🪞

In 1 week you will hear the difference.

Say this sentence in a voice message and I will check it 🎙

speaking.title: The TH sound
speaking.subtitle: Do you say “sink” when you mean “think”?
rows: Put the tip of your tongue **between your teeth**
speaking.caption: A TH mistake changes the meaning: think and sink 🚢 Practise in front of a mirror. You should see your tongue. Can you say “Three thousand thirty-three”? 😄

speaking.title: Where is the stress?
speaking.subtitle: Wrong stress = people don't know the word
speaking.caption:
If you are not sure, check the stress in a dictionary 📖

The Cambridge Dictionary has audio for every word.

Which word do you always get wrong? 👇

speaking.title: The robot voice
speaking.subtitle: Every sentence in the same tone = Pronunciation 6
rows: Your voice **goes up** at the end of a yes/no question
It **goes down** at the end of a sentence
speaking.caption:
Repeat an English podcast out loud and copy the tone too 🎶

Intonation is the secret of Band 7 pronunciation.

Have you ever recorded your voice and listened to it? 👇

speaking.title: Fast ≠ fluent
speaking.subtitle: When you are nervous and speak fast, words get lost
speaking.caption:
Being clear comes first 🥇

If the examiner can't understand you, even the best words give no points.

Do you speak fast? 👇

speaking.title: Don't stop at every mistake
speaking.subtitle: Correcting all the time lowers your Fluency
rows: Starting the sentence again after every mistake
**Don't fix** a small mistake, just go on
A big mistake: fix it **fast**: “I go, sorry, I **went**.”
speaking.caption:
Fluency matters more than being perfect 🌊

Native speakers make mistakes too, and they keep going.

Do you correct yourself a lot? 👇

speaking.title: Good, bad, nice...
speaking.subtitle: Basic words = Lexical 5.5
speaking.caption:
One strong adjective is better than “very + a basic adjective” 💪

Today, use 2 of these words in a conversation.

Which ones will you choose? 👇

speaking.title: Idioms: be careful
speaking.subtitle: “Raining cats and dogs” is old-fashioned
rows: Pushing an idiom into your answer
Use one only where it is **natural** and **correct**
**a piece of cake, once in a blue moon, on the go**
speaking.caption:
A wrong idiom is worse than no idiom 😬

Choose modern phrases that people really use.

What is your favourite idiom? 👇

speaking.title: Phrasal verbs
speaking.subtitle: Formal words sound strange in Speaking
rows: **look forward to** = wait for something with joy
speaking.caption: Phrasal verbs make your speech natural and raise your vocabulary score 📈 Bonus: get on with = have a good relationship with. Save this 🔖

speaking.title: More than “I think”
speaking.subtitle: Don't start every answer the same way
speaking.caption:
Different phrases = better Lexical Resource ⬆️

Make it a habit to start each Part 3 answer in a new way.

Which one do you use the most? 👇

speaking.title: Different grammar
speaking.subtitle: Only Present Simple = Grammar 6
rows: **“If” sentence**: If I had more time, I'd travel more.
**Used to**: I used to play football.
speaking.caption: Different tenses and structures = Band 7 grammar 🎓 Bonus: a relative clause, like a friend who lives abroad. Which structure do you use the most? 👇

speaking.title: City or countryside?
speaking.subtitle: A one-word answer = a lost chance
rows: “I'd **much rather** live in the city, mainly because it's **far more** convenient.”
“**Having said that**, the countryside is **much less** stressful.”
speaking.caption: much / far / a lot + a comparative = a strong comparison 💪 Talking about the two sides is a sign of Band 7. Where would you like to live? Write in English 👇

speaking.title: The future is not only “will”
speaking.subtitle: Structures for future plans
speaking.caption:
4 ways to start your answer to “What will you do after university?” 🚀

Different structures show the examiner your grammar range.

What is your plan? Write in English 👇

speaking.title: Childhood habits
speaking.subtitle: “When I was a child, I play...”
rows: “We **would** spend every summer at my grandparents'.”
speaking.caption:
Questions about childhood come up a lot in Part 1 and Part 2 🧒

“Used to” and “would” are your best friends.

What did you do as a child? Write in English 👇

speaking.title: The hobby question
speaking.subtitle: “I watch films.” Not enough
rows: “I usually **head to** the mountains near Chimgan.”
“It's a great way to **clear my head**.”
speaking.caption: into, head to, clear my head = natural, living language 🏔 Prepare 3 sentences like these about your own hobby. What is your hobby? 👇

speaking.title: Work or study?
speaking.subtitle: “I'm a student.” And that's all
rows: “I'm **currently in my third year** at university...”
speaking.caption: This is the first question of Part 1, so it is your first impression ✨ demanding, rewarding = Band 7 words. What do you study, or where do you work? Write in English 👇

speaking.title: About your city
speaking.subtitle: “Tashkent is big and beautiful.” Weak
rows: “...with a mix of **Soviet-style** buildings and modern **skyscrapers**.”
“**What I like most** is the food.”
speaking.caption:
Formula: describe the place + give your own opinion 🏙

Prepare an answer like this about your own city.

Where are you from? 👇

speaking.title: Describing a person
speaking.subtitle: How they look is not enough
rows: **Who** they are and how you met
**The effect on you**: “She made me realise that...”
speaking.caption:
“Describe a person who inspired you” is one of the most common cards 🌟

Prepare one person before the exam.

Who inspires you? 👇

speaking.title: Describing a place
speaking.subtitle: “It was beautiful.” Beautiful how?
rows: “The streets were filled with **the smell of freshly baked bread**.”
speaking.caption:
The 5 senses method = the examiner can see the place in their mind 🖼

It raises your Lexical Resource at once.

Describe your favourite place in one sentence 👇

speaking.title: Describing an object
speaking.subtitle: You finish in 40 seconds
rows: **History**: when and how you got it
speaking.caption:
30 seconds for each = 2 minutes ⏱

Prepare one object for “Something you own that is important to you”.

What important thing do you own? 👇

speaking.title: Bring the event to life
speaking.subtitle: Add details and dialogue
rows: An exact **time**: “a freezing evening last January”
speaking.caption:
Dialogue makes your story feel like a film 🎬

Try it with “Describe a time when you helped someone”.

Have you ever helped someone? 👇

speaking.title: Don't forget the last point
speaking.subtitle: “...and explain why” is the most important part
rows: Talking about 2 of the 4 points on the card
**Explain why** gives you the most to say
speaking.caption:
“Explain why” = feelings and opinions = the most points 🎯

Don't leave it for the end. You may run out of time.

Do you get to the last point? 👇

speaking.title: The examiner stopped you?
speaking.subtitle: That is a good sign!
rows: The examiner **always** stops you when time is up
speaking.caption:
Stay calm and get ready for the next question 😌

Being stopped is a sign of success.

Did you know this? 👇

speaking.title: Feeling nervous
speaking.subtitle: Your hands shake and the words don't come
rows: Speak English for **5 minutes** before the exam
speaking.caption:
Feeling nervous is normal, and you can control it 🧘

After the first 2 minutes you usually calm down.

Do you get nervous in exams? 👇

speaking.title: “What about you?”
speaking.subtitle: Don't ask the examiner personal questions
rows: This is an **interview**, not a normal chat
Ask only if you **don't understand** the question
speaking.caption:
The examiner will not answer, and it feels uncomfortable 😶

Keep the focus on your own answer.

Did you know this? 👇

speaking.title: You can change your mind
speaking.subtitle: You started with the wrong idea?
rows: This is a sign of **natural speech**
speaking.caption:
Changing your mind does not hurt your Fluency 🔄

Native speakers do it too.

Save this 🔖

speaking.title: “It depends” + silence
speaking.subtitle: This is a start, not an answer
speaking.caption:
After “it depends”, always give examples 📋

This is a perfect structure for Part 3.

Do you use “it depends” a lot? 👇

speaking.title: Guessing about the future
speaking.subtitle: “How will education change?”
speaking.caption:
Part 3 has a lot of these questions 🚀

If you know these phrases, a hard question becomes easy.

How do you think education will change? Write in English 👇

speaking.title: Past vs now
speaking.subtitle: “How has shopping changed?”
rows: “**In the past**, people **used to** shop at bazaars.”
“**These days, however**, more people order online.”
**used to + these days** = a perfect pair
speaking.caption:
Questions about change are a Part 3 classic 🔄

Use this formula for any topic.

What has changed in your city? 👇

speaking.title: “Yes, I agree.” is not enough
speaking.subtitle: There are levels of agreeing
rows: “I agree **to some extent**, but...” = partly agree
“**I see their point**, but...” = a polite way to disagree
speaking.caption:
Showing the level = careful thinking = a higher score 🎓

Then, of course, give a reason.

Which one do you use? 👇

speaking.title: Don't repeat the question
speaking.subtitle: “Do you like music?” “Yes, I like music.”
rows: Repeating the **exact** words of the question
“**Absolutely**, I'm a **big fan**, especially of jazz.”
“I **can't live without it**, to be honest.”
speaking.caption:
A synonym = a chance to show your Lexical Resource 🎯

Listen to the question and answer it in different words.

Do you like music? Answer in English 👇

speaking.title: Start with confidence
speaking.subtitle: Every answer starts with “Umm... yes...”
speaking.caption:
The first word gives you confidence, and the next sentences come easily 🚀

Learn these 4 starts. They fit any question.

Which one do you like? 👇

speaking.title: Reading ≠ speaking
speaking.subtitle: You read the topics but never speak out loud
rows: A Part 2 card: **1 minute to plan, 2 minutes to speak**
speaking.caption:
Record it on your phone and listen again 🔁

Speaking gets better only by speaking.

Will you speak for 10 minutes today? 👇

speaking.title: Listen to yourself
speaking.subtitle: You don't know your own mistakes
speaking.caption:
Hearing your own voice for the first time is strange, but very useful 😅

The second try is always better.

Have you tried it? 👇

speaking.title: Practise with a partner
speaking.subtitle: Preparing alone does not teach you live conversation
rows: 2 times a week, play **examiner and candidate**
Use a timer and tell each other **one main mistake**
speaking.caption:
A speaking partner = the best free teacher 🤝

If you are looking for a partner, find each other in the comments 👇

Who is looking for a partner?

speaking.title: Part 1 topics
speaking.subtitle: They come back again and again, so be ready
speaking.caption:
Prepare 10 words and 1 personal story for each one 📒

Part 1 = easy points, if you are ready.

Which topic is the hardest for you? 👇

speaking.title: Stories for every card
speaking.subtitle: You don't need a new story for each card
rows: A story about a **present** or a **success**
speaking.caption:
One travel story fits the cards “a place”, “a happy memory” and “a journey” 🔁

5–6 stories = ready for 50+ cards.

What is your story for every card? 👇

speaking.title: “Furthermore” is for writing
speaking.subtitle: Speak in a natural way in Speaking
speaking.caption:
Speaking is a conversation, not an essay 🗣

Writing phrases sound strange when you speak.

Have you used “moreover” in Speaking? 😅

speaking.title: I do not know → I don't
speaking.subtitle: Speech with no short forms = a robot
rows: “I do not know. I am not sure. It is good.”
In Speaking, short forms **help your score**
speaking.caption:
No short forms in Writing, but in Speaking, yes ✅

They make your speech smooth and natural.

Did you know this? 👇

speaking.title: Ready-made chunks
speaking.subtitle: Building every sentence word by word is slow
speaking.caption:
These chunks give your brain time and make you speak faster ⚡

Learn and use 2 new chunks a day.

Which chunk do you use the most? 👇

speaking.title: Show that you care
speaking.subtitle: A bored voice about your favourite hobby
speaking.caption:
The examiner also feels how well you communicate 🎭

It comes naturally when you talk about something you like.

What topic makes your eyes light up? 👇

speaking.title: Eye contact
speaking.subtitle: Speaking to the table
rows: It is not marked directly, but it helps you **speak smoothly**
speaking.caption:
Looking confident helps you speak with confidence 💪

When you practise, look at your partner too.

Is eye contact hard for you? 👇

speaking.title: Warm up
speaking.subtitle: Silent all morning = hard first answers
rows: Listen to a podcast for **15 minutes** before the exam
Talk to yourself **in English** on the way
speaking.caption:
Your speaking muscles need a warm-up too 🏃

An athlete does not start a game with no warm-up. You should not start the exam that way.

What do you do before an exam? 👇

speaking.title: The 4 marking criteria
speaking.subtitle: Know how you are marked
speaking.caption:
Each one is 25% ⚖️

Record yourself and give a mark from 1 to 9 for each one.

Which one is your strongest? 👇

speaking.title: Fluency is not speed
speaking.subtitle: Fluency is speech that keeps going and makes sense
speaking.caption:
A logical flow matters more than speed 🧠

Linking phrases keep your speech in order.

How do you link your ideas? 👇

speaking.title: You don't know the topic?
speaking.subtitle: “Describe a piece of art.” And you don't care about art
rows: Bring the topic **closer to your life**
A photo on your phone, **graffiti**, a book cover
Be honest: “I'm **not really into** art, but...”
speaking.caption:
You can link any card to your own life 🔗

Being creative is the secret weapon of Speaking.

What was your hardest card? 👇

speaking.title: Finish clearly
speaking.subtitle: Your talk just stops, and the examiner waits
rows: “**So yeah**, that's why I love it.”
“**So, all in all**, it was a great experience.”
speaking.caption:
A clear ending tells the examiner that you have finished ✅

No uncomfortable silence, just a nice full stop.

Save this 🔖

speaking.title: Don't leave Speaking for later
speaking.subtitle: It is the slowest skill to grow
speaking.caption:
A daily habit works better than a weekly marathon 🔥

Start today: 15 minutes, any topic.

How many weeks are left before your exam? 👇

speaking.title: Think in English
speaking.subtitle: Translating makes you speak slowly
rows: Thinking in your own language first, then **translating**
Describe the things around you **in English, in your head**
“I'm waiting for the bus. **It's late again**.”
speaking.caption:
5 minutes a day = in 3 weeks you translate less 🧠

It is the simplest exercise, and the strongest.

Describe what is around you now in one English sentence 👇
